title: Accurate Failure Prediction in Agents Does Not Imply Effective Failure Prevention
authors: Vasudev, Rakshith; Russak, Melisa; Bikel, Dan; Alshikh, Waseem
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: A binary critic scores live prefixes; temperature scaling adjusts confidence before rollback or appended guidance. The study separates recovery of otherwise failing runs from disruption of otherwise successful ones, and uses a 50-task pilot to predict whether deployment will help.
findings: Offline AUROC 0.94 coexists with a 26-percentage-point success collapse in one setting; high-failure ALFWorld gains 2.8 points. Outcomes depend on the backbone and baseline success rate.
design: Task-disjoint train/validation/test partitions; ALFWorld is absent from critic training. Intervention sweeps and heuristic controls support a deployment comparison rather than only offline classification.
gap: The predictor-to-policy distinction is already demonstrated. Two simple intervention modes do not identify a general action-specific optimal policy; a global go/no-go pilot is narrower than local benefit estimation.
future: Estimate action-specific net benefit with replicated checkpoint branches, and test confidence-bound decisions against a fixed threshold at equal total budget.
role: Principal conceptual baseline; prevents an AUROC-only novelty claim.
evidence_location: Sections on critic calibration, intervention results, pilot test, and limitations.

title: Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart: Early Failure Prediction and Restart for SWE Agentic Tasks
authors: Wang, Chenyu; Lyu, Yunbo; He, Junda; Yang, Zhou; Zhong, Chenxing; Harel, Yaniv; Lo, David
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: A 0.6B black-box monitor learns terminal and dense fail-to-pass supervision from observable prefixes. An alarm starts a same-policy run with a clean prompt history. Stable partial edits are offered as an optional diff, so the new attempt can inspect, apply, or reject them.
findings: At a target 5% false-positive rate, transferred monitoring saves 14.6–20.4% execution tokens. At a 25% target, Qwen resolution rises from 66.6% to 71.8%, versus 66.8% for cold restart. The higher-success operating point adds net token cost.
design: Frozen 350/50/100 instance-grouped split keeps repetitions together; 100 held-out tasks × five runs support paired comparisons. Training on Qwen transfers to three policies, including a closed API.
gap: Transfer can succeed: PreAct cannot claim all monitors fail across agents. Restart and artifact reuse are established; a fixed restart policy does not learn which feasible intervention is best.
future: Compare monitor representations on identical traces and budgets; add verification and abstention controls, reporting any overhead beyond saved execution tokens.
evidence_location: Experimental setup, threshold calibration, Tables on stopping and restart, deployment limitations.

title: PrefixGuard: Online Failure Warning and Trace-Grounded Diagnosis for LLM Agents
authors: Huang, Xinmiao; Hu, Jinwei; He, Qisong; Roy, Rajarshi; Wu, Changshun; Dong, Yi; Huang, Xiaowei
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Under Review
target: Horizon-specific terminal warning and rule violations
summary: Learned event adapters convert heterogeneous traces into a GRU risk sequence. A risk-labeled deterministic finite automaton provides symbolic replay and rule inspection. First-alert thresholds use successful calibration trajectories, linking ranking to an explicit alarm budget.
findings: The inspected v2 reports superior mean AUPRC in 24 benchmark–horizon settings, with gains of 12.0–21.9 points. At nominal 10% FAR, horizon-averaged recall spans 56.1–93.0%. Rule checking identifies violations in 21 of 265 successful tau²-Bench runs.
design: Its allocator keeps each held-out task represented in training. This is held-out trajectory evaluation, not unseen-task or held-out-agent evidence. Validation selects checkpoints; a separate calibration set freezes alarms.
gap: Online warning and symbolic diagnosis are prior work. The paper explicitly leaves unseen tasks/agents and controlled correction unmeasured; a successful terminal label can conceal rule violations.
future: Use task-disjoint and agent-disjoint splits, then randomize corrections at pre-action checkpoints while separating terminal success from constraint satisfaction.
role: Principal horizon-aware predictor comparator; important split-design contrast.
evidence_location: v2 Appendix B split allocation and calibration; conclusion.

title: When Evidence is Sparse: Weakly Supervised Early Failure Alerting in Dialogs and LLM-Agent Trajectories
authors: Baidya, Avinash; Liang, Xinran; Guo, Ruocheng; Gao, Xiang; Das, Kamalika
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 9 pages, 14 figures, and appendix
domain: Dialog, support, tool use and planning
summary: An attention model learns which turns carry failure evidence from terminal labels instead of labeling every prefix equally. A preference-conditioned alpha-STOP policy chooses an accuracy–earliness operating point without retraining a separate trigger for each preference.
findings: Across five benchmarks, relevant evidence occupies 4.7–11.3% of turns and first appears after 59.0–83.6% of trajectories on average. Predictor frontier hypervolume improves 1–10%; the combined system improves 3–42% over compared triggers.
design: The benchmark mixture includes non-agent dialog data. Frontier quality concerns prediction and timing, not successful rescue. Evidence relevance is model-derived, not a causal-error timestamp.
gap: Terminal labels are weak supervision for actionable warnings. Sparse attention is not proof of the earliest recoverable point, and an early alert does not establish benefit.
future: Compare sparse supervision with adjudicated onset and recoverability labels; report calibration and resumed outcomes at fixed alarm budgets.
evidence_location: Evidence-sparsity analysis, predictor/trigger experiments, limitations.

title: AgentForesight: Online Auditing for Early Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Zhang, Boxuan; Zhu, Jianing; Shi, Zeru; Liu, Dongfang; Tang, Ruixiang
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 33 pages, 7 figures
domain: Multi-agent coding, math and agentic tasks
target: Decisive error boundary and responsible agent
summary: A specialized 7B auditor reads only each unfolding prefix and predicts whether a decisive error has appeared, where it lies, and who contributed. AFTraj-2K pairs safe traces with injected unsafe variants and consensus-derived critical-step labels.
findings: Reported comparisons include gains up to 19.9% against selected judges and substantially lower step-localization error. External Who&When tests probe transfer beyond its construction pipeline.
design: The v2 split groups each safe trajectory with its injected variants, preventing sibling leakage. The external benchmark is disjoint; this does not isolate an unseen backbone from all other changes.
gap: Boundary detection is at or near an error already occurring. It cannot be renamed pre-error prevention; injected and consensus labels require executable and organic-failure checks.
future: Test prefix alarms before the harmful action, report lead time relative to executable onset, and measure corrective value with monitor-call overhead included.
evidence_location: v2 evaluation protocol, external Who&When experiment, Appendix G limitations.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
authors: Zheng, Xu; Chen, Zhuomin; Lin, Chaohao; Wei, Hua; Chen, Haifeng; Cheng, Wei; Luo, Dongsheng
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Risk of the proposed next action
summary: Historical action trajectories form a probabilistic graph; a learned graph debugger evaluates the current proposed action and returns feedback before execution. External structural information helps the same agent self-correct, reducing dependence on parametric introspection alone.
findings: The paper reports average pass-ratio improvement of 14.69% across four benchmarks and three agents. Pass ratio and grounding ratio are distinct outputs and need separate interpretation.
design: Benchmarks use explicit task/variant partitions and multiple backbone comparisons. Testing several backbones is not automatically a frozen monitor trained without the target agent. Historical graphs remain an input requirement.
gap: Pre-execution warning plus self-correction already exists. Graph coverage, new actions and environment changes may limit deployment; a single feedback mechanism does not establish optimal action selection.
future: Compare frozen cross-agent graphs with domain-adapted graphs, test cold start, and audit false disruption under matched compute.
role: Required pre-action baseline; rules out generic pre-execution novelty.
evidence_location: Section 5 experimental setup, pass/grounding comparisons and graph construction.

title: Atropos: Improving Cost-Benefit Trade-off of LLM-based Agents under Self-Consistency with Early Termination and Model Hotswap
authors: Kim, Naryeong; Yoo, Shin
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Will appear at ISSTA 2026
target: Eventual failure of parallel inference paths
summary: A graph convolutional predictor scores merged parallel paths. Predicted weak-model failures terminate early, and surviving context can be handed to a stronger model. The method evaluates cost-benefit tradeoffs under multi-path/self-consistency execution.
findings: Reported midpoint accuracy is about 0.85; hotswap converts up to 27.57% of predicted failures. A reported operating point reaches 74.35% of closed-model performance at 23.9% of its cost.
design: Model replacement is an intervention, not evidence that a frozen monitor transfers to an unseen agent. Some expensive stronger-model baseline costs/performance are extrapolated; compare measured and estimated quantities separately.
gap: Early stopping and escalation are prior work. Parallel-path assumptions and estimated baseline costs complicate direct comparison to a single active software-agent run.
future: Repeat all cost baselines with direct execution, vary model prices, and test single-run escalation against cheap verification at common budgets.
role: Model-switching and cost comparator, conditional on matching its execution regime.
evidence_location: Prediction/hotswap experiments and threats to validity.

title: EarlyEval: Cheaper Agent Evaluation via Early Outcome Prediction
authors: Shi, Yuling; Sun, Zhensu; Dong, Junsen; Wan, Chengcheng; Lo, David; Gu, Xiaodong
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Code and data available at this https URL
summary: Two LightGBM heads predict success and failure from behavior, text and reference-solution metadata. Monotonic calibration rescales confidence; threshold halting reduces benchmark execution while preserving aggregate resolve rates and model ranking.
findings: Reported savings span 13–26% of steps, up to 44.1% input tokens and 29.4% output tokens, at 89–97% accuracy. Resolve-rate shifts average roughly 1–2 points.
design: Leave-one-agent-out evaluation directly tests an unseen agent. Reference-free ablations are relevant for deployment, because benchmark solutions are not normally available to a live assistant.
gap: Outcome imputation for cheaper evaluation is different from task completion. Omitted reference features can change performance; aggregate ranking preservation does not certify every run or target calibration.
future: Reproduce the reference-free variant on task-disjoint data and measure completion after intervention, rather than counting a predicted verdict as a solved task.
role: Strong inexpensive predictor and positive transfer evidence.
evidence_location: Research questions, Section III calibration/features, leave-one-agent-out results.

title: AgentStop: Terminating Local AI Agents Early to Save Energy in Consumer Devices
authors: Pham, Dzung; Katevas, Kleomenis; Shamsabadi, Ali Shahin; Haddadi, Hamed
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ACM CAIS '26
domain: Local web QA and SWE agents
target: Likely unsuccessful run and energy waste
summary: A lightweight supervisor uses execution signals including token log probabilities to stop unpromising local-agent trajectories. Hardware measurements connect agent reasoning and repeated execution to GPU power, heat and battery use.
findings: The paper reports 15–20% energy saving with less than 5% task-utility loss in evaluated settings. Energy savings are measured on consumer hardware and are not interchangeable with token savings.
design: Threshold sweeps expose a utility–efficiency frontier. Closed APIs may not expose log probabilities. The discussion explicitly leaves transfer across horizons, prompts and reasoning depths uncertain.
gap: Cancellation trades success for resources; it is not recovery. Useful partial state may be lost and model access requirements limit portability.
future: Test black-box feature variants and checkpoint salvage, with joules, wall time, tokens and final completion reported separately.
evidence_location: Hardware experiments, early-stop results, Discussion 8.1.

title: Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction
authors: Cho, Seonglae; Fernandez, Franklin Cardenoso; Mohammed, Umar; Wu, Zekun; Da Costa, Kleyton; Wicaksono, Ilham; Koshiyama, Adriano
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: An activity abstraction compresses a corpus into a finite-state machine. Per-state behavioral features support failure classification, while state context predicts subsequent actions. The automaton captures shared harness-level execution structure.
findings: Reported machines contain 7–43 states and replay held-out traces with fitness at least 0.997. Failure AUROC reaches 0.94 in some settings; replay fitness is not prediction accuracy.
design: Experiments use dataset-specific abstractions and 80/20 partitions. Broad dataset coverage does not itself establish frozen leave-agent/scaffold-out monitoring. The machine accepts a directly-follows closure, not the true generating language.
gap: Structural regularity can encode harness shortcuts. Bigram-preserving adversarial traces may replay, and high ranking need not yield calibrated alarms or useful intervention.
future: Fit abstractions on source scaffolds only; test unseen schemas and goal semantics, including adversarial topology-preserving failures.
role: Structural representation comparator close to PreAct features.
evidence_location: Setup, failure-prediction experiments, Section 6 limitations.

title: Testing-Driven Reliability Audit of Trajectory-Based Early Outcome Prediction for LLM Agents: Target-Specific Calibration Transfer Persists Within a Single Benchmark
authors: Cao, YanZe
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 26 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: A frozen dual-head prediction pipeline is audited with leave-one-agent-out and shared-predictor leave-two-agent-out controls. Oracle prior correction is a diagnostic, while task resampling, training cohorts and jackknife tests probe persistence.
findings: Broad pairwise heterogeneity does not pass the prespecified criterion. Two target/head cells retain corrected gaps 0.1377 and 0.1107. TerminalBench does not establish cross-benchmark replication; one head makes no qualifying decisions.
design: Holding a predictor fixed across targets separates target behavior from changes in training cohort. Oracle correction uses information unavailable as a routine deployment feature.
gap: The result is target-specific, not proof that every agent transfer fails or that the model alone causes it. This already studies calibration transfer, restricting PreAct novelty.
future: Compare target-specific recalibration and abstention with prior-only adjustment, estimating success and coverage under common stopping rules.
role: Mandatory calibration/transfer predecessor; motivates a narrower replication contribution.
evidence_location: Abstract, shared-predictor controls, persistence battery and boundary-test results.

title: ProbGuard: Proactive Runtime Monitoring for LLM Agent Safety via Probabilistic Prediction
authors: Wang, Haoyu; Poskitt, Christopher M.; Wei, Jiali; Sun, Jun
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Accepted by the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Symbolic abstractions and a learned discrete-time Markov chain estimate the probability of remaining safe. Semantic validity constraints and a PAC-style sample analysis support the abstraction, while threshold crossing activates re-prompting or halting.
findings: Warnings precede driving violations by up to 15.84 seconds at one zero-observed-false-alarm setting. Embodied re-prompting reduces unsafe behavior 65.37% while retaining 80.4% of baseline completion; stricter halting has a larger completion cost.
design: Safety outcomes and task completion are explicitly distinct. Assumptions about state abstraction and model certification must be respected; a finite sample with zero alarms is not a universal guarantee.
gap: Anticipatory runtime safety is established, including intervention. Ordinary task rescue and broad model/scaffold transfer remain separate questions.
future: Add goal-completion labels and evaluate safety/completion Pareto tradeoffs under schema shift and changing dynamics.
role: Formal reachability precedent; use a separate safety target.
evidence_location: v4 safety/intervention experiments and probabilistic abstraction; author reports ASE 2026 acceptance.

title: When Agents go Astray: Course-Correcting SWE Agents with PRMs
authors: Gandhi, Shubham; Tsay, Jason; Ganhotra, Jatin; Kate, Kiran; Rizk, Yara
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Online trajectory inefficiency and course correction
summary: An inference-time process reward model identifies redundant exploration, loops and missed termination. Taxonomy-guided feedback steers execution without updating the base policy; ablations compare unguided and explicit next-action prescriptions.
findings: A reported setup improves resolution from 40.0% to 50.6% and reduces trajectory length relative to some feedback alternatives. Additional inference cost can be as low as $0.2 in that setup.
design: The result evaluates a policy-plus-monitor combination, not a general failure probability. Agent strength and feedback wording affect the relevant comparison.
gap: Online correction already changes task success. Benefits from one backbone cannot be assumed for stronger policies; benign exploration may be misread as inefficiency.
future: Measure disruption/recovery separately and test feedback against same-policy restart and verification, matching total inference cost.
role: Direct intervention baseline; moved from adjacent to Category 1.
evidence_location: Inference-time framework and feedback strategy experiments.

title: Real-Time Detection and Repair of LLM Agent Failures
authors: Dubey, Sunny
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 16 pages, 5 figures. Code, data and demo: this http URL Walkthrough: this http URL
domain: Synthetic telemetry, booking tools, AFTraj-2K, ATBench
summary: A one-class echo-state-network/CUSUM ensemble learns healthy telemetry. Deterministic grounding and tool-contract checks complement behavioral alarms. Failed booking runs are rolled back to a fact-gathering checkpoint and repaired under several feedback policies.
findings: Synthetic-study AUROC is 0.872; cold cross-family monitoring is 0.527 versus 0.885 after target recalibration. On the 120-episode booking study, located repair raises success about 52% to 73%; conditional recovery is 45% versus 16% for resampling.
design: Synthetic, injected live, external-corpus and repair cohorts have different denominators. Paired repair uses identical prefixes and repeated live calls. The paper and current repository differ on some p-values and verification counts; this extraction uses the paper.
gap: Matched-prefix repair, transfer failure and recalibration are already present. Detection often follows onset; narrow recomputable tasks and injected faults limit generalization. Adaptive repair is not significantly better than resampling in this study.
future: Test organic software failures before onset, factorial model/scaffold holdouts, and prespecified utility-based selection against the located-repair policy at equal total cost.
role: Most consequential newly added comparator; sharply narrows claimed novelty.
evidence_location: Synthetic result table, deployment transfer, Section 9 repair table and Section 11 limitations.

title: ProMAS: Proactive Error Forecasting for Multi-Agent Systems Using Markov Transition Dynamics
authors: Zhao, Xinkui; Liu, Sai; Zhang, Yifan; Ma, Qingyu; Cheng, Guanjie; Wang, Naibo; Liu, Chang
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: Causal Delta Features encode semantic displacement into a quantized Vector Markov Space. A prediction head and jump detector use risk acceleration to flag critical reasoning changes before the complete log is consumed.
findings: The reported step-level accuracy is 22.97% while inspecting 27% of reasoning logs, a 73% reduction in data inspected. This is localization accuracy, not failure AUROC or task-success gain.
design: Evaluation uses a failure-attribution benchmark and compares latency/accuracy against reactive and post-hoc methods. Fewer consumed logs do not by themselves prove a positive lead time before error.
gap: Semantic predictive multi-agent monitoring is prior work. Log reduction and localization do not establish calibrated risk or successful prevention.
future: Report the alert position relative to annotated error, success-run false alarms, and randomized remediation with monitored agent execution.
evidence_location: Method, Who&When experiment and accuracy/latency comparison.

title: A Self-Healing Framework for Reliable LLM-Based Autonomous Agents
authors: Jeong, Cheonsu; Shin, Younggun
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ISSN (online): 1793-6403
summary: Reliability assessment combines output consistency, semantic correctness and execution success. Abnormal patterns trigger adaptive replanning or corrective prompts, providing an integrated detection/recovery workflow rather than a separate future-horizon predictor.
findings: Although the abstract claims improvements, Section 4.4 says experiments are currently being conducted and comprehensive results will follow. The inspected version supplies no completed quantitative result table; recovery gains must not be treated as established.
design: The proposed setup uses task-specific reliability weights and a 0.65 preliminary threshold. This is retained as an inherited framework reference, an explicit exception to empirical-study eligibility.
gap: A reliability score is not a calibrated failure probability. Completed validation, sample counts, uncertainty and quantitative recovery effects remain missing in the inspected version.
future: Compare identical recovery actions triggered before versus after executable onset, using held-out tasks and a separately frozen threshold.
evidence_location: Sections 3–4 framework, setup, baselines and evaluation.

title: AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories
authors: Barke, Shraddha; Goyal, Arnav; Khare, Alind; Singh, Avaljot; Nath, Suman; Bansal, Chetan
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Accepted to EMNLP Findings 2026
domain: 11 API, incident and web/file task settings
summary: Constraints synthesized from a failed trajectory are checked step by step. A validation log supplies explicit evidence to a judge, which localizes the critical step and failure category. Manual grounded-theory annotation supports a cross-domain taxonomy.
findings: The dataset contains 170 failed trajectories; reported step-localization improvement averages 75% over prior work. The judge may abstain as inconclusive when evidence is weak.
design: This evaluates diagnosis conditioned on a known failed run. Three-run result variation and category definitions are reported; future trajectory evidence is available during retrospective constraint synthesis.
gap: The diagnostic pipeline cannot be used online unchanged. No success controls means its diagnosis accuracy is not an alarm false-positive rate.
future: Mask future observations, add successful controls and compare prefix-only constraint synthesis with terminal diagnosis before evaluating rescue.
role: Source of failure labels and auditable diagnostics.
evidence_location: Benchmark construction, judging experiments and Section 7 limitations.

title: ToolPRMBench: Evaluating and Advancing Process Reward Models for Tool-using Agents
authors: Li, Dawei; Yao, Yuguang; Tan, Zhen; Liu, Huan; Guo, Ruocheng
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: under review
summary: Each test case contains history, a correct action, a plausible wrong alternative and tool metadata. Offline sampling isolates single-step errors; online rollout sampling captures accumulated mistakes. Multi-model verification reduces label noise.
findings: The appendix lists 987 cases: 542 training and 445 test. General PRMs often fail to exceed 55% average accuracy, motivating tool-specialized supervision.
design: Some source benchmarks appear only in testing. The principal experiment is intrinsic PRM discrimination, not full search-policy improvement; multi-LLM labels are not infallible.
gap: Choosing the locally better action does not estimate eventual failure, recoverability or intervention effect. The authors explicitly limit extensive end-to-end search evaluation.
future: Resume both action alternatives from the same checkpoint and measure terminal outcomes, cost and cross-tool calibration.
role: Action-risk component and local correctness benchmark.
evidence_location: Main discrimination experiments, Limitations and Appendix A split table.

title: AgentLens: Revealing The Lucky Pass Problem in SWE-Agent Evaluation
authors: Sahoo, Priyam; Mittal, Gaurav; Li, Xiaomin; Ma, Shengjie; Steenhoek, Benjamin; Lin, Pingping; Hu, Yu
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: Task-specific prefix-tree references merge multiple passing runs. History-sensitive intent labels distinguish exploration, implementation, verification and orchestration, supporting process quality, divergence and waste analyses.
findings: From 2,614 trajectories over eight models and 60 tasks, 47 tasks support a 1,815-trace reference-based subset. In that subset, 10.7% of passing runs are classified as Lucky Passes.
design: Post-hoc scoring relies on passing references for the same task, unavailable for a new issue. Subset eligibility changes the denominator; quality ranking is not a failure classifier.
gap: An anomalous process can still succeed. Treating process defects as terminal failure labels would introduce target mismatch and may penalize valid exploration.
future: Test deployment-available intent features on unseen tasks and predict waste, defects and terminal resolution as separate targets.
evidence_location: Dataset construction, process-tier experiments and Appendix A limitations.

title: PROACT-Agent: Progressive Runtime Oversight and Active Circuit-breaking for Real-Time Safety
authors: Jia, Ding; Liu, Wei; Du, Xianglong; Li, Yingjie; Yang, Yingqing; Yu, Huili; Zhan, Zhangsong; Zhou, Chu
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Unsafe state and exact safety boundary
summary: Progressive trajectory unrolling and causal rectification enforce temporal consistency of safety labels. A runtime guard evaluates updated context before the next model inference; localized bilingual variants probe safety across language contexts.
findings: PROACT-Bench has 155,780 states. Under source holdout, unsafe F1 is 91.46% and boundary detection 90.63%; non-DoS targeted attack success in AgentDojo drops from 20.82% to 0.40%.
design: Canonical roots group derived prefix, rationale and language variants. Source holdout differs from agent holdout. Synthetic adjudicated safety labels and attack-specific outcomes are separate from task resolution.
gap: Safety-boundary consistency is relevant, but interception after malicious content is observed is not ordinary failure prevention. No classifier offers universal protection.
future: Adapt temporal consistency checks to organic task-error annotations; measure benign-task disruption and generalization outside attack sources.
role: Temporal label construction and safety boundary comparator.
evidence_location: Canonical-root/source split table, held-out safety and AgentDojo results.

title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents
authors: Wang, Haoyu; Poskitt, Christopher M.; Sun, Jun
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Proc. ICSE'26, pages 2938-2950. ACM, 2026
domain: Code execution, embodied agents and driving
summary: A domain-specific language expresses triggers, predicates and enforcement actions. Rules block, modify or constrain unsafe behavior with interpretable checks, providing a deterministic layer alongside stochastic policies.
findings: Evaluated rules prevent over 90% of unsafe code cases and all hazardous embodied actions in the tested scenarios; driving compliance reaches 100% in the evaluated configuration. Generated-rule coverage is weaker than curated-rule coverage.
design: Those percentages concern specified scenario populations, not all future unsafe executions. Millisecond enforcement overhead is measured; policy quality and rule completeness are distinct.
gap: Known constraints can be enforced without learned prediction, but unseen semantic task failures may lack executable predicates. Safety compliance is not calibrated task-failure forecasting.
future: Compare rule checks, learned monitors and combined gates on organic tool failures, with separate rule coverage and task-disruption statistics.
evidence_location: Runtime DSL, evaluation and generated-rule experiments; record reports ICSE 2026 publication.

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
authors: Liu, Jiale; Xi, Huajun; Zhang, Shaokun; Zeng, Yifan; Yue, Tianwei; Wang, Chi; Kang, Jian; Wu, Qingyun; Wang, Huazheng
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: A controlled pipeline exactly replays a successful prefix before injecting a fault. Golden labels support attribution across modalities and protocols, addressing ambiguity in natural failed logs.
findings: The paper introduces 12,326 failed trajectories and analyzes attribution behavior across model families, modalities and protocols.
design: Injection provenance supplies a known boundary. The dataset is conditioned on induced failures; causal labels reflect the injected intervention, not every naturally arising multi-cause failure.
gap: A known injected step does not guarantee natural-failure validity or successful-run warning calibration. Attribution after a fault differs from prediction before it.
future: Use successful parent traces as grouped controls; validate on adjudicated organic errors and quantify the injection-to-natural transfer gap.
role: Event-time label source and replay-validity precedent.
evidence_location: Controlled construction pipeline and benchmark analysis.

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Zhang, Shaokun; Yin, Ming; Zhang, Jieyu; Liu, Jiale; Han, Zhiguang; Zhang, Jingyang; Li, Beibin; Wang, Chi; Wang, Huazheng; Chen, Yiran; Wu, Qingyun
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: camera-ready
summary: Fine-grained failed logs support automated attribution via all-at-once, binary-search and stepwise methods. The study separates responsibility for an unsuccessful task from locating the pivotal reasoning step.
findings: The best method reaches 53.5% responsible-agent accuracy but only 14.2% decisive-step accuracy; strong reasoning models remain unreliable for practical attribution.
design: Labels support debugging completed failures. The evaluation is not a prefix warning trial and excludes the successful-run population needed for alarm calibration.
gap: Error localization is difficult and labels may require complete traces. Training an online monitor on these labels needs explicit masking and onset definitions.
future: Assess annotator uncertainty, prefix-only localization and interventional confirmation rather than treating one step as uniquely causal.
role: Failure-attribution benchmark behind several newer monitors.
evidence_location: Dataset and attribution comparisons; inspected camera-ready v3.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors: Cemri, Mert; Pan, Melissa Z.; Yang, Shuyi; Agrawal, Lakshya A.; Chopra, Bhavya; Tiwari, Rishabh; Keutzer, Kurt; Parameswaran, Aditya; Klein, Dan; Ramchandran, Kannan; Zaharia, Matei; Gonzalez, Joseph E.; Stoica, Ion
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ArXiv v3
summary: Expert analysis of 150 traces yields fourteen failure modes grouped into system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. A validated judge scales annotations across a larger multi-agent corpus.
findings: MAST-Data contains over 1,600 traces. Reported expert agreement is kappa 0.88; failures often reflect coordination and verification rather than one isolated model error.
design: This is an empirical taxonomy, not a prospective predictor. Annotator agreement measures label consistency, not causal validity or monitor recall.
gap: Failure categories can guide features but do not provide prevention windows. System-level causes may not be attributable to one recoverable local action.
future: Annotate when each mode first becomes observable and test interventions specific to coordination versus capability versus verification failures.
role: Failure modes and multi-agent feature design.
evidence_location: Taxonomy construction, annotation validation and cross-framework analysis.

title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
authors: Zhao, Xiangxin; Li, Han; Li, Shuaiting; Zhao, Tianyi; Barr, Earl T.; Sarro, Federica; Ye, He
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: The study treats coding failure as a developing sequence of decisions and observations rather than only a final unresolved patch. It analyzes recurring phases and behavioral patterns in CLI-agent traces.
findings: Of 3,843 traces from seven frontier models and three scaffolds on Terminal-Bench, 1,794 valid complete traces (over 63,000 steps) receive manual annotation. Fourteen findings indicate predominantly epistemic errors, often beginning early but becoming visible late.
design: A retrospective trajectory study can associate behaviors with outcome without demonstrating that those features are visible early or causally repairable.
gap: Patterns can reflect scaffold logging, task difficulty or selection on final outcome. A descriptive association does not establish an online risk score.
future: Freeze prefix-only features from its taxonomy, test task/agent holdouts, and validate candidate mechanisms with controlled edits to the execution policy.
evidence_location: Empirical setup, trajectory analyses and limitations; findings refined from full-text extraction.

title: From Plan to Action: How Well Do Agents Follow the Plan?
authors: Liu, Shuyang; Dehghan, Saman; Ganhotra, Jatin; Hirzel, Martin; Jabbarvand, Reyhaneh
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: The paper compares declared plans with subsequent actions, analyzing how plan quality, reminders and execution choices affect programming-agent behavior. It supplies evidence for plan deviation as a candidate monitor signal.
findings: The inspected v3 analyzes 21,120 SWE-agent trajectories across four models, two SWE benchmarks and eight plan variations. Standard plans and reminders help in evaluated settings; subpar plans and some added early phases hurt. Older bibliography counts are superseded.
design: Plan generation and reminders are evaluated as agent-policy interventions. A deviation may be beneficial adaptation to new evidence, so compliance labels require context.
gap: A strict plan-deviation feature risks false alarms when the original plan is wrong. Plans differ in granularity and scaffold presentation.
future: Separate justified revision from unexplained drift, and test whether a deviation signal predicts added verification value beyond tool errors and task difficulty.
role: Plan-deviation feature backing with a target-mismatch caution.
evidence_location: Plan/action assessment, reminder experiment and threats to validity.

title: Abduct, Act, Predict: Scaffolding Causal Inference for Automated Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: West, Alva; Weng, Yixuan; Zhu, Minjun; Lin, Zhen; Ning, Zhiyuan; Zhang, Yue
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: A single LLM inference is scaffolded to abduct hidden causes, propose a minimal correction and imagine the subsequent trajectory. Full conversation context supports causal-style reasoning, without requiring actual environment execution of the imagined branch.
findings: Step accuracy is 47.46% versus 16.67% on 126 algorithm-generated cases, and 29.31% versus 12.07% on 58 hand-crafted cases. These are attribution results, not measured rescue rates.
design: The correction and outcome are mentally simulated inside the model. This is not an executable interventional identification design, despite causal terminology.
gap: Causal-style prompting is already established. Imagined outcomes can be wrong; PreAct must distinguish hypothetical attribution from actual branch execution and randomization.
future: Reuse active hypothesis verification in live prefixes, recording legality, replayability and downstream outcome for each intervention.
evidence_location: Abduct/act/predict framework and attribution evaluation.

title: DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Ma, Ming; Zhang, Jue; Yang, Fangkai; Kang, Yu; Lin, Qingwei; Rajmohan, Saravan; Zhang, Dongmei
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: Failure hypotheses are tested by targeted interventions such as changing a plan or editing a message. Outcome progress replaces a single responsible-step label, because distinct repairs may independently solve the same failed task.
findings: Reported recovery is 18–28% on failed GAIA/AssistantBench trials, with up to 16% milestone progress and 30–60% of hypotheses validated/refuted; AG2/GSMPlus recovery is 49%.
design: These are conditional failed-trial recovery rates, not population success gains. Cross-framework evidence supports debugging portability but does not establish a frozen predictive monitor.
gap: Outcome-oriented and intervention-validated debugging are established. Recovery after completed failure does not choose an early beneficial interruption point.
future: Compare diagnostic interventions at matched live checkpoints and include untouched successful runs to estimate disruption and net utility.
evidence_location: Framework, dataset-specific recovery and hypothesis-validation results.

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
authors: Zhu, Kunlun; Liu, Zijia; Li, Bingxuan; Tian, Muxin; Yang, Yingxuan; Zhang, Jiaxun; Han, Pengrui; Xie, Qipeng; Cui, Fuyang; Zhang, Weijia; Ma, Xiaoteng; Yu, Xiaodong; Ramesh, Gowtham; Wu, Jialian; Liu, Zicheng; Lu, Pan; Zou, James; You, Jiaxuan
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Failure explanation and learning from feedback
summary: A failure-analysis framework organizes recurring agent errors and converts diagnoses into feedback intended to improve subsequent execution. The work connects error analysis with corrective agent behavior.
findings: AgentErrorBench spans ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop. Average all-correct attribution rises from 0.3% to 24.3%, and exact step accuracy from 28% to 45%. Iterative targeted feedback improves task success by up to 26% relative, not 26 percentage points.
design: Diagnosis and feedback may use completed trajectories. Their availability at a proposed action must be checked before using them as online features.
gap: Improving later attempts is different from rescuing the current run. Fault labels can mix local symptoms with upstream causes.
future: Evaluate masked-prefix feedback, compare to simple reflection/retry, and retain a same-policy resampling control.
evidence_location: Failure taxonomy, AgentDebug framework and benchmark experiments.

title: TRAIL: Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization
authors: Deshpande, Darshan; Gangal, Varun; Mehta, Hersh; Krishnan, Jitin; Kannappan, Anand; Qian, Rebecca
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Dataset: this https URL
summary: A trace-based benchmark evaluates how well models identify and explain agentic execution issues. It provides structured error-analysis tasks and a reusable setting for diagnostic reasoning.
findings: TRAIL contains 148 human-annotated traces from single- and multi-agent systems. The reported best Gemini-2.5-Pro score is 11%; this benchmark score is not warning accuracy or failure AUROC.
design: Post-hoc issue analysis can see information that a live monitor cannot. Its labeled unit is an issue in a trace, rather than an independent task-level intervention outcome.
gap: Trace reasoning quality does not show early detection or recovery value. Errors may be valid labels without a unique intervention point.
future: Build prefix masks and success controls, then use executable checks to test whether the identified issue is actionable.
evidence_location: Benchmark construction and model localization evaluation.

title: AgentNoiseBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents Under Noisy Condition
authors: Wang, Ruipeng; Chen, Yuxin; Wang, Yukai; Wu, Chang; Fang, Junfeng; Cai, Xiaodong; Gu, Qi; Su, Hui; Zhang, An; Wang, Xiang; Cai, Xunliang; Chua, Tat-Seng
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
summary: The benchmark perturbs the external conditions faced by tool agents and evaluates robustness. It separates environmental noise from reasoning capability and exposes how corrupted observations affect execution.
findings: The study distinguishes user noise from tool noise and preserves task solvability during injection. Its primary comparison reports an average accuracy drop of 20.8% under noise; the measure is task accuracy, not monitor discrimination.
design: Controlled noise permits systematic stress tests. Perturbation realism, severity and dependence on tool schemas limit extrapolation to organic failures.
gap: Noise sensitivity is not an online alarm policy. A monitor can spuriously learn injection artifacts rather than semantic contradiction.
future: Evaluate intervention policies on both injected and naturally noisy runs, and compare tool-contract checks with semantic inconsistency scores.
role: Stress-test environment and observation-quality feature backing.
evidence_location: Noise construction and robustness experiments.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
authors: Yao, Shunyu; Zhao, Jeffrey; Yu, Dian; Du, Nan; Shafran, Izhak; Narasimhan, Karthik; Cao, Yuan
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: v3 is the ICLR camera ready version with some typos fixed. Project site with code: this https URL
summary: Interleaved reasoning and environmental actions allow a language model to gather evidence, track plans and revise decisions. Tool observations reduce hallucination and error propagation compared with reasoning in isolation.
findings: Reported interactive success gains over imitation/reinforcement baselines are 34 points on ALFWorld and 10 on WebShop in the original setup.
design: These are historical backbone-specific agent comparisons, not current frontier performance or a separate failure-monitor evaluation.
gap: ReAct supplies observable prefixes but no calibrated monitor, alarm threshold or action-specific interruption value.
future: Attach monitors without changing base-agent prompts; measure marginal benefit over a strong ReAct-like policy at matched budget.
evidence_location: ICLR camera-ready v3 methods and interactive results.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
authors: Shinn, Noah; Cassano, Federico; Berman, Edward; Gopinath, Ashwin; Narasimhan, Karthik; Yao, Shunyu
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: v4 contains a few additional experiments
summary: An agent stores linguistic reflections from scalar or textual task feedback in episodic memory. Later trials condition on that memory without updating model weights.
findings: The paper reports 91% HumanEval pass@1 in one configuration versus the cited GPT-4 baseline of 80%; this is not a repository-agent early-warning result.
design: Reflection sources and memory ablations clarify the learning mechanism. Historical benchmark conditions and repeated attempts must be matched in any comparison.
gap: Feedback after an attempt is not evidence of beneficial interruption during one. Poor reflections may anchor a new rollout on a wrong diagnosis.
future: Compare reflection, clean restart and artifact reuse at identical checkpoint budgets, with feedback correctness audited.
evidence_location: Framework and reflection/memory ablations.

title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
authors: Lù, Xing Han; Kazemnejad, Amirhossein; Meade, Nicholas; Patel, Arkil; Shin, Dongchan; Zambrano, Alejandra; Stańczak, Karolina; Shaw, Peter; Pal, Christopher J.; Reddy, Siva
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Evaluator validity, success and side effects
summary: Expert reviewers annotate success, side effects and repetition in completed web trajectories. Twelve language-model judges are compared against those labels and conventional rule-based evaluators.
findings: The benchmark has 1,302 trajectories from four agent LLMs. No judge dominates across all five environments; common rule-based checks can undercount success.
design: Evaluator agreement concerns label quality. An expert success label and an executable state verifier each have limits; side effects need a separate outcome.
gap: A monitor may learn benchmark-checker artifacts. Noisy terminal labels can distort both training and alarm calibration.
future: Audit contested outcomes, annotate side effects independently, and run sensitivity analyses under executable and expert labels.
evidence_location: Expert annotation and LLM/rule evaluator comparisons.

title: Model-Based Runtime Monitoring with Interactive Imitation Learning
authors: Liu, Huihan; Dass, Shivin; Martín-Martín, Roberto; Zhu, Yuke
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
target: Future risky states and human assistance
summary: A latent dynamics model simulates future policy actions, and a failure classifier predicts risk. Human interventions provide supervision without requiring dangerous failures; the policy and monitor improve through interactive imitation learning.
findings: Reported success gains are 23% in simulation and 40% on hardware against compared baselines; robot-specific human-workload measures improve as deployment data accumulate.
design: The environment admits learned transition dynamics; human intervention labels reflect perceived risk. It is a cross-domain precedent, not direct tool-language-agent evidence.
gap: Semantic APIs, nondeterministic external services and irreversible actions make reliable language-agent simulation harder than latent robot-state rollout.
future: Use checkpoint/replay where valid and explicit abstention where a tool effect cannot be simulated; audit human-help burden separately.
evidence_location: Dynamics/failure-model design and system-level experiments.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
authors: Zhou, Shuyan; Xu, Frank F.; Zhu, Hao; Zhou, Xuhui; Lo, Robert; Sridhar, Abishek; Cheng, Xianyi; Ou, Tianyue; Bisk, Yonatan; Fried, Daniel; Alon, Uri; Neubig, Graham
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Our code, data, environment reproduction resources, and video demonstrations are publicly available at this https URL
summary: Reproducible websites, tools and long-horizon goals create a realistic browser-agent evaluation setting. Functional terminal checks establish a task-level success endpoint.
findings: The original best GPT-4 agent reaches 14.41% success versus 78.24% for humans; these historical figures motivate difficulty and are not a current model ranking.
design: Self-hosting permits state snapshots but requires careful reset and task independence. Evaluation predicates do not necessarily capture every acceptable user outcome.
gap: Benchmark success alone supplies no causal-error timestamp or intervention-effect label.
future: Add replayable checkpoints, event-time annotations and harmless-success controls for a cross-domain PreAct trial.
evidence_location: Environment/task construction and baseline evaluation.

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
authors: Liu, Xiao; Yu, Hao; Zhang, Hanchen; Xu, Yifan; Lei, Xuanyu; Lai, Hanyu; Gu, Yu; Ding, Hangliang; Men, Kaiwen; Yang, Kejuan; Zhang, Shudan; Deng, Xiang; Zeng, Aohan; Du, Zhengxiao; Zhang, Chenhui; Shen, Sheng; Zhang, Tianjun; Su, Yu; Sun, Huan; Huang, Minlie; Dong, Yuxiao; Tang, Jie
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Published in ICLR 2024
summary: A multi-environment benchmark tests language models as agents and analyzes failures in long-term reasoning, decision making and instruction following.
findings: The paper documents a capability gap between evaluated commercial and open models and releases environments and an integrated evaluation package.
design: Benchmark diversity is not a single comparable outcome or failure-monitor training distribution. Environment-specific scoring and horizons matter.
gap: Aggregate scores hide the onset and mechanism of failure. A general capability benchmark cannot substitute for a task-disjoint monitor test.
future: Choose one reproducible environment first, then test the monitor on genuinely held-out environments with matched label definitions.
evidence_location: ICLR 2024 benchmark design and failure analysis.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
authors: Jimenez, Carlos E.; Yang, John; Wettig, Alexander; Yao, Shunyu; Pei, Kexin; Press, Ofir; Narasimhan, Karthik
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Data, code, and leaderboard are available at this https URL ICLR 2024, this https URL
summary: Repository issues and human-authored fixes define realistic software tasks. Tests assess whether generated patches resolve an issue, moving evaluation beyond isolated function completion.
findings: The benchmark contains 2,294 issue instances drawn from 12 Python repositories in its original release. Historical model baselines demonstrate substantial difficulty.
design: Tests define an operational endpoint, not all dimensions of patch quality. Repository overlap, contamination and repeated attempts require grouped evaluation.
gap: A failed test outcome does not label first error or show whether a live-prefix action could rescue the run.
future: Track branch states and full budgets, use repository/task holdouts, and audit patch side effects and verifier adequacy.
evidence_location: Dataset construction and execution-based evaluation.

title: SWE-bench Goes Live!
authors: Zhang, Linghao; He, Shilin; Zhang, Chaoyun; Kang, Yu; Li, Bowen; Xie, Chengxing; Wang, Junhao; Wang, Maoquan; Huang, Yufan; Fu, Shengyu; Nallipogu, Elsie; Lin, Qingwei; Dang, Yingnong; Rajmohan, Saravan; Zhang, Dongmei
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: Homepage: \url{ this https URL }, Code: \url{ this https URL }, Dataset: \url{ this https URL }
summary: A continuously refreshed software-engineering benchmark seeks to reduce contamination and staleness while preserving executable task environments and comparable evaluation.
findings: Its release and baseline evaluations support freshness-aware software-agent testing; the exact current inventory is version-dependent and should be frozen before experiments.
design: A changing benchmark requires dataset-version identifiers, environment manifests and compatible task predicates. Refreshing tasks alone does not ensure no leakage.
gap: Temporal freshness does not establish monitor transfer or causal prevention. Version drift can masquerade as model change.
future: Run a temporal holdout with frozen artifacts, separating time shift from agent/scaffold shift and reporting retention of calibration.
evidence_location: Inspected v2 benchmark pipeline and evaluation.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
authors: Guo, Chuan; Pleiss, Geoff; Sun, Yu; Weinberger, Kilian Q.
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ICML 2017
summary: Modern neural classifiers can be confidently wrong. Post-hoc temperature scaling adjusts logits using held-out data, distinguishing probability accuracy from class discrimination.
findings: The study finds temperature scaling effective across evaluated architectures and datasets; it does not establish robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
design: The methodological evidence predates tool agents. A monotonic calibrator preserves ranking and cannot repair AUROC below chance.
gap: In-domain calibration is not a certificate for a new tool scaffold, and threshold calibration is different from measuring full probabilistic reliability.
future: Report Brier/reliability and decision coverage by deployment; recalibrate only with separate target data and preserve an untouched target test split.
role: Calibration foundation; contextual exception to the 2022 start date.
evidence_location: Calibration metrics and temperature-scaling experiments.
